column2: The men bring up and bring in the covenant ark to Aminadab's hill house, then consecrate Eleazar to guard it; both occurrences of the full covenant designation remain.
The multiplied days reach twenty years, and all Israel's house looks toward the Lord. The duration and whole-house subject remain rather than adding a separate period of mourning.
column3: Looked to is a readable interpretation of epeblepsen with opiso; the following-after direction and possible devotional implications remain open.

column2: Whole-hearted return is conditional, followed by removal of foreign gods and groves, preparation of hearts and service to Him alone, with promised rescue from the foreigners' hand. Alone is explicit mono.
Baalim and groves of Astaroth are removed, followed by service to the Lord alone. The selected cultic objects are not reduced to a generic statement of repentance.
Samuel directs the gathering of all Israel at Mizpah and promises prayer for them to the Lord; ordinary human pronouns remain appropriate.
Drawing and pouring water before the Lord, fasting that day, confession and Samuel's judging at Mizpah remain separate acts. No explanation of the water rite is added to the text.
The foreigners hear of the complete gathering, their satraps go up against Israel, and Israel hears and fears; the paired hearing sequence remains.
The double negative construction asks Samuel not to be silent by ceasing to cry; keep crying makes that request intelligible. The people's expectation is that the Lord will save them.
One nursing lamb, whole burnt offering with all the people, Samuel's cry for Israel and the Lord's hearing him remain; with all the people follows the selected explicit phrase.
The foreigners approach while the offering is underway; the Lord's great thunderous voice precedes their confusion and fall before Israel. Divine action is not reduced to weather alone.
Israel's men leave Mizpah, pursue and strike the foreigners as far as below Beth-chor; the endpoint's below and selected name remain.
One stone is set between Mizpah and the old city, named Ebenezer with the explicit gloss Stone of the Helper, then interpreted by Samuel's Thus far saying.
column3: City supplies a noun for the substantival feminine old; the geographic identification is not resolved by the Greek running text alone.

column2: The Lord explicitly humbles the foreigners, their further entry is negated, and His hand remains against them all Samuel's days. Again is supported by the added further-entry construction.
Restoration and returning of cities are both retained, with the selected Ashkelon-to-Azob extent, recovery of territory and peace with the Amorite.
column3: The plural subjects of returned and recovered are not both explicitly named; the English they preserves that ambiguity rather than inventing a diplomatic transaction.

column2: Samuel's judging lasts all the days of his life; the inherited throughout his life expresses the full temporal scope.
Year-by-year travel circles Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, with judgment in all these consecrated places. The unusual consecration descriptor is not replaced by generic locations.
Return to Armathaim is explained by his house there, followed by judging there and building an altar there; the repeated locality remains audible.
Samuel's old age precedes his appointing his sons judges for Israel; no assessment of their conduct is imported before verse 3.
Joel is firstborn and Abijah second, with both judges in Beersheba. The naming order and location remain explicit.
The sons' failure to walk in his way, turning after completion, receiving gifts and bending ordinances remain. Bribes is the contextual rendering of gifts in judicial corruption.
column3: The inherited completion for synteleia is provisional and unusually opaque; fiscal gain/contribution senses require lexical investigation, not a silent substitution based on another language's reading.

column2: Israel's men gather and come to Samuel at Armathaim; men is retained without substituting elders from a different textual tradition.
Behold, old age and the sons' failed example motivate the request for a king to judge like the other nations; ordinary human you remains throughout.
The request is evil in Samuel's eyes, is quoted again, and prompts prayer to the Lord. His evaluation and prayer remain distinct narrative steps.

Propose restoring the explanation's For and the source's not you but Me order before the purpose of not reigning. Treating as nothing repeats the Greek contempt verb; divine first-person Me and ordinary address to Samuel remain.
column3: The purpose clause describes the people's rejection; the proposal does not claim that the desired end had already occurred.

column2: All deeds from departure from Egypt to this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, establish the comparison with what they are doing to Samuel as well. The first-person divine grievance remains.
The command to listen is qualified by solemnly testifying and reporting the king's claim. Solemnly carries the emphatic cognate construction rather than omitting its force.
column3: Claim for dikaioma is a contextual provisional choice; right or practice remains a lexical alternative without asserting divine approval of every royal taking.

column2: Samuel transmits the whole word of the Lord to the people requesting a king; the transmission's complete scope is explicit.
The king's claim begins with taking sons for chariots, cavalry and running before chariots. Repeated his and your distinguish royal benefit from the people's loss.
Thousand- and hundred-commanders precede harvesting, vintage gathering, weapon making and chariot equipment. No plowing clause is supplied from a familiar parallel text.
Daughters are taken for three occupations: perfuming, cooking and baking. The distinct tasks remain rather than generic household service.
Fields, vineyards and good olive groves are taken and given to the king's servants. Good remains attached to the olive groves in the inherited syntax.
The king tithes seed and vineyards for eunuchs and servants; these are separate named recipient groups, not generalized officials alone.

Male slaves, female slaves, good cattle herds and donkeys are taken, followed by tithing for his works. The selected cattle herds and tithe verb remain rather than replacing them with young men and putting to work.
The tithe extends to flocks and culminates in you becoming his slaves; yourselves marks the explicitly expressed plural pronoun without changing its referent.
The people's cry because of their chosen king meets the Lord's refusal to hear in those days; their choosing a king for themselves is repeated as the explanation.
The people's unwillingness to hear Samuel introduces an emphatic denial and insistence that a king shall be over them. There must be conveys their insistence rather than a narrator's necessity claim.
Being like all nations is followed by the king's judging, going out before them and fighting their war; all three expected functions remain.
Samuel hears all the people's words and speaks them into the Lord's ears; the bodily hearing image is retained rather than replaced by a generic report.
The Lord commands listening and making a king reign for them; Samuel then dismisses each man to his city. The two speakers and distinct commands remain clear.
